module_title: Meaning of Inflation and Types Based on Speed
introduction: Inflation is simply the 'sustained increase in the general price level of goods and services' over a period of time. When prices rise, the 'purchasing power' of money falls. At this level, we will classify inflation based on how fast prices are rising.

core_concepts.title: 1. Creeping Inflation
core_concepts.description: When prices rise at a very slow and predictable rate (usually 2% to 3% annually). Economists consider this 'good and necessary' for a developing economy because it encourages producers to manufacture more goods and hire more workers.

core_concepts.title: 2. Walking (Trotting) Inflation
core_concepts.description: When the rate of inflation falls between 3% and 10%. It serves as a 'warning signal' for the government and the Central Bank (RBI) to start tightening monetary policy before the situation gets out of hand.

core_concepts.title: 3. Galloping Inflation
core_concepts.description: When inflation starts jumping in double or triple digits (10% to 100% or more). It is dangerous for the economy. Money loses its value so fast that people stop holding cash and start buying real assets like gold or real estate to protect their wealth.

core_concepts.title: 4. Hyperinflation
core_concepts.description: An uncontrollable situation where prices rise by millions or billions of percent per month. Paper currency completely loses its value, and people need wheelbarrows of cash just to buy a loaf of bread (Classic historical examples: Zimbabwe in 2008, Germany in 1923, and recently Venezuela).

important_entities.name: Purchasing Power
important_entities.significance: Inflation and purchasing power have a strict inverse relationship. As inflation goes UP, the purchasing power of your currency goes DOWN. (A ₹100 note buys fewer goods today than it did 10 years ago).

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: A common misconception tested in exams. A 0% inflation rate or negative inflation is actually terrible for an economy (it leads to stagnation). A mild 'Creeping Inflation' is the optimal, healthy state for an economy.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: A baby first Creeps, then Walks, then a horse Gallops, and finally goes Hyper. (Creeping -> Walking -> Galloping -> Hyperinflation).

exam_strategy_tips: Direct trivia question: 'The economic crisis in Zimbabwe where a 100 Trillion dollar note was printed is an example of what?' Answer: Hyperinflation.
